sections.overview: Papilio demodocus, the Citrus Swallowtail, is widespread across sub-Saharan Africa and is also recorded on nearby Arabian land and Socotra.
sections.identification: Its dark wings carry prominent yellow bands and spots, with the hindwing tails typical of swallowtails. Young caterpillars can resemble bird droppings.
sections.habitat: It occupies many sub-Saharan habitats, including gardens and other human-modified places; the regional assessment excludes deserts and Afro-alpine environments.
sections.diet: Caterpillars use a broad range of citrus and other Rutaceae as food plants. Adults feed on flower nectar.
sections.behavior: When threatened, the caterpillar can expose an osmeterium, a forked scent organ characteristic of swallowtail larvae.
sections.reproduction: Females lay eggs on larval food plants; caterpillars grow through successive moults and then pupate. Timing depends on local conditions.
sections.ecology: Like the Orchard Swallowtail, Papilio aegeus, this species belongs to Papilio and its caterpillars use Rutaceae; their ranges and recorded hosts differ, so the two are not interchangeable.
sections.conservation: The 2022 IUCN assessment lists it as Least Concern, citing its wide range, use of altered habitats and cultivated larval food plants.
